text: Two architectures both get called quantum applications, and mixing them up leads teams to budget, staff, and schedule a project completely wrong. Knowing which one you're building, before you write a line of code, decides almost everything downstream.

We'll define Pattern A, the coprocessor pattern from the last two lessons, and Pattern B, quantum as the whole program. Then we'll classify a real problem into one or the other, and see exactly what changes between them — team skills, cost model, testing strategy, and whether it's actually production-ready today.

Pattern A's hardware looks like this: a short list of devices you call into for one bounded sub-task — evaluating a cost function, sampling a distribution — architecturally identical to how a GPU gets called from a classical machine-learning pipeline.

And here's Amazon Braket's real Algorithm library — a catalog of the quantum algorithms people actually run. The overwhelming majority of what's deployed in finance, chemistry, and logistics pilots today is Pattern A. Pattern B — a complete algorithm as one circuit, no classical feedback loop, like Grover's search or Shor's factoring run as textbook algorithms — shows up constantly in papers but almost never in production.

Here's why: this is a real result from IBM Quantum's own hundred-qubit GHZ experiment, showing the measured signal decaying with distance because of noise. Pattern B needs far more qubits and far lower error rates than exist today. Pattern A sidesteps that, because a classical optimizer can tolerate and correct for noisy intermediate results in a way a single one-shot circuit can't.

Take the same business problem — find the best routing for twenty delivery trucks — and look at both architectures. Pattern A formulates it as a QUBO, feeds it to a QAOA loop with a classical optimizer driving parameter updates: buildable today. Pattern B would try to encode the entire search as one circuit whose single measurement gives the optimal route directly — that needs a scale of fault-tolerant qubits that simply doesn't exist yet. The business problem didn't decide the architecture. The hardware did.
Next lesson puts both patterns to work on three real tickets — the kind that actually show up in a backlog, underspecified and a little ambiguous.
